steps.label: SPREAD = sigma / sqrt(n)
steps.sub: 4x the data only halves the spread

eyebrow: A skewed exponential population, averaged at n = 1, 5, 30, 100
caption: Real simulation output: the same right-skewed data, turning symmetric as n grows.
Center never shifts from ~40. Spread matches the sigma/sqrt(n) prediction almost exactly.

code:
# n    mean(means)  std(means)  predicted  skew
# 100   40.06         4.07         4.00     0.24

# "n >= 30" is a rule of thumb, not a law --
# this skewed data still shows leftover asymmetry at n=30
caption: By n=100 the shape is visibly symmetric -- but very skewed data may need hundreds.

code:
means = rng.choice(pop, size=(5000, 30)).mean(axis=1)
se = pop.std() / np.sqrt(30)
print(round((abs(means - pop.mean()) < 1.96 * se).mean(), 4))
# 0.9518
caption: n=30 is a rule of thumb, not a law -- here it still gives ~95.2% coverage, decently close.
